prompt: Standard Precautions in dentistry mean staff should

options.text: Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
Apply PPE and extra precautions for patients with a known bloodborne infection
Treat blood as infectious but handle saliva as noninfectious unless visibly bloody
Change gloves between patients but skip hand hygiene when gloves were worn

explanation: Standard Precautions assume unknown infectious status; gloves do not replace hand hygiene. This includes using appropriate PPE and hand hygiene with every patient.

distractorExplanations.b: Precautions keyed to disclosed infection status are outdated; Standard Precautions apply to every patient because status is often unknown.
distractorExplanations.c: In dentistry saliva is treated as potentially infectious material; the bloody-saliva exception belongs to old Universal Precautions outside dentistry.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves can have micro-defects and hands get contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene is still required after gloves come off.

Instead of eye protection during splash procedures
Only as a fashion accessory

distractorExplanations.c: Eye protection is separate for splashes.
distractorExplanations.d: Respirators are PPE, not fashion.

prompt: Hand hygiene should be performed

options.text: After removing gloves at the end of each patient, but not before gloving
Only when hands are visibly soiled, since glove use covers routine contact
Before donning gloves, after removing gloves, and whenever hands are contaminated
At the start and end of each shift, with glove changes covering patient contacts

distractorExplanations.b: Visible soil is the trigger for soap and water, not the only trigger; gloves never replace hand hygiene before and after patient care.
distractorExplanations.d: Shift-based hand hygiene ignores the per-patient moments around gloving; a glove change without hand hygiene leaves hands contaminated.

prompt: Which PPE combination is most appropriate for a procedure likely to produce splash of blood/saliva?

explanation: Mucous membrane and clothing protection match splash risk. Eye protection may be goggles or a face shield.

distractorExplanations.a: The assistant sits in the same spatter zone as the operator, so eye protection is required for everyone exposed, not just the operator.
distractorExplanations.b: The mask protects the nose and mouth from blood/saliva splash on every spatter-generating procedure, not only for respiratory symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: A face shield can replace eyewear, but CDC still calls for a mask under it because spatter travels around the shield to the nose and mouth.

prompt: Which item is considered a critical instrument (Spaulding) requiring sterilization?

Mouth mirrors that touch mucous membranes
Amalgam condensers that contact oral tissue

explanation: Critical items contact sterile tissue/vasculature and require sterilization. Examples include surgical instruments and periodontal scalers.

distractorExplanations.b: Mouth mirrors contact mucosa without penetrating tissue, which makes them semicritical items under the Spaulding classification.
distractorExplanations.c: CDC lists amalgam condensers as semicritical: they touch mucous membranes but do not penetrate soft tissue or bone.

prompt: Semicritical instruments (contact mucous membranes) should be

explanation: Semicritical items need sterilization or HLD depending on material tolerance. Follow the manufacturer's IFU for heat-sensitive items.

prompt: Spill cleanup of blood on a clinical surface should include

options.text: PPE, then disinfectant sprayed on the blood and wiped off immediately
Absorbent removal, then a quick wipe with 70% alcohol as the disinfectant
PPE, then a sterilant such as glutaraldehyde applied to the counter
PPE, absorbent removal of bulk soil, then EPA-registered disinfectant

explanation: Clean then disinfect with proper wet time. Leave the disinfectant wet for its labeled contact time.

distractorExplanations.a: Skips removal of bulk blood and ignores contact time; organic soil inactivates disinfectant and immediate wiping prevents kill.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol evaporates before achieving contact time and is not recommended by CDC as a surface disinfectant for blood spills.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterilants and high-level disinfectants are not intended for environmental surfaces; use an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant.

prompt: Which statement about disinfection vs sterilization is correct?

options.text: Disinfection reduces pathogens; sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores
High-level disinfection and sterilization both kill spores reliably at standard contact times
Sterilization reduces pathogens to safe levels; disinfection destroys all microbial life on items
Disinfection destroys spores given enough contact time; sterilization just shortens the process

explanation: Spaulding and CDC distinguish disinfection levels from sterilization.

distractorExplanations.b: High-level disinfection kills most microbes but not high numbers of bacterial spores at standard contact times; only sterilization does.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the definitions: disinfection reduces pathogens, while sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores.
distractorExplanations.d: Surface disinfectants are not sporicidal at labeled times; sterilization is a different level of kill, not a faster disinfection.

prompt: Operatory cleanup between patients should prioritize

options.text: Disinfecting housekeeping surfaces such as floors before clinical surfaces
Removing barriers, cleaning/disinfecting clinical contact surfaces
Spraying surfaces with disinfectant and placing barriers before wiping
Wiping surfaces with a dry towel, then covering them with fresh barriers

explanation: Systematic between-patient IPC protects the next patient. Sharps and waste are also managed safely during turnover.

distractorExplanations.a: Floors and walls are low-risk housekeeping surfaces; between-patient priority is clinical contact surfaces and barriers.
distractorExplanations.c: Surfaces must be precleaned and the disinfectant left for its contact time before new barriers go on.
distractorExplanations.d: Dry wiping does not disinfect; contaminated surfaces need cleaning and an EPA-registered disinfectant before re-barriering.

prompt: Clinical contact surfaces that may be contaminated should be

options.text: Disinfected once at day's end if no blood was visible during care
Covered with barriers, which are left in place for the full day
Barrier-protected and/or cleaned and disinfected between patients
Sprayed with disinfectant and covered with a barrier without precleaning

explanation: CDC/OSAP-aligned practice: barriers and/or disinfection between patients. Use an appropriate EPA-registered product.

distractorExplanations.a: Spatter and gloved-hand contact contaminate surfaces with every patient, visible blood or not; treat them between patients.
distractorExplanations.b: Barriers are changed between patients; a day-long barrier carries contamination from one patient to the next.
distractorExplanations.d: Precleaning removes organic soil that inactivates disinfectant; spray-and-cover skips both cleaning and contact time.

prompt: Housekeeping surfaces (floors, walls) typically require

options.text: Disinfection between every patient with an intermediate-level product
Monthly cleaning, since they rarely contact patients' hands
The same EPA hospital disinfectant schedule as clinical contact surfaces
Routine cleaning; more frequent disinfection when visibly soiled

explanation: Housekeeping surfaces are cleaned routinely; intensive disinfection when soiled. Disinfect promptly when soiled with blood or body fluids.

distractorExplanations.a: Per-patient intermediate-level disinfection is the rule for clinical contact surfaces, not for floors and walls.
distractorExplanations.b: Low contact does not mean monthly; housekeeping surfaces are cleaned on a regular schedule and when soiled.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the two surface categories; housekeeping surfaces need routine cleaning, not the clinical between-patient schedule.

prompt: Dental unit waterlines should be maintained so water quality

options.text: Meets dental water standards (eg, ≤500 CFU/mL heterotrophic bacteria for non-surgical use)
Is sterile for every procedure because tap water cannot be used in dental units
Is acceptable once lines are flushed for 20–30 seconds at the start of each clinic day
Is checked by the unit's in-line filter, which removes the need for water testing

explanation: Waterline biofilms need active management and monitoring. Flushing and waterline treatment protocols maintain that level.

distractorExplanations.b: Sterile water is required only for surgical procedures; nonsurgical care uses water meeting the ≤500 CFU/mL standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Flushing helps but does not eliminate biofilm; CDC still expects waterline treatment and periodic monitoring.
distractorExplanations.d: In-line filters reduce bacteria but can fail or be colonized; monitoring is still needed to confirm water quality.

prompt: Regulated medical waste (e.g., sharps) must be

options.text: Recapped with two hands and placed in a red bag with gauze
Placed in appropriate puncture-resistant containers
Placed in a sealed red bag lined with a second plastic bag
Collected in an empty plastic bottle, then sealed in the regular trash

explanation: Sharps and regulated waste have specific containment/disposal rules. Handle and dispose of them per OSHA and state rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping is prohibited, and red bags are not puncture-resistant enough to contain sharps.
distractorExplanations.c: Double bags still tear on needles and blades; sharps require closable, leak-proof, puncture-resistant containers.
distractorExplanations.d: Improvised bottles are not labeled sharps containers, and regulated sharps waste cannot go in ordinary trash.

prompt: After a blood spill on a counter, you should

options.text: Disinfect with a low-level product first, then clean up the remaining blood afterward
Wipe with a damp towel, then apply a sterilant such as glutaraldehyde
Contain, clean, and disinfect with an appropriate intermediate-level disinfectant
Cover with a barrier film and disinfect at the end of the clinic day

explanation: Blood spills need proper cleaning/disinfection. Follow the office protocol for spills.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the order (clean first, then disinfect) and uses low-level instead of intermediate-level disinfectant for blood.
distractorExplanations.b: Sterilants are for semicritical devices, not environmental surfaces; spills need an EPA-registered intermediate-level product.
distractorExplanations.d: Blood spills are cleaned and disinfected promptly; covering them leaves infectious material on the surface.

options.text: Establish an exposure control plan, offer HBV vaccination, provide PPE, and train employees
Establish an exposure control plan and require HBV vaccination as a condition of hire
Provide PPE and annual training, with HBV vaccination costs paid by the employee
Train employees every three years and review the exposure control plan as needed

prompt: After a needlestick from a used instrument, the employee should

options.text: Squeeze the site to bleed it, apply bleach, and report at the end of the day
Wash the site, report immediately, and follow post-exposure evaluation
Wash the site, then report only if the patient's history shows HIV or hepatitis
Wash the site and start PEP within 7 days if the source tests positive

explanation: Timely reporting enables PEP decisions and documentation. Prophylaxis decisions follow the post-exposure protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Squeezing and caustic agents are not recommended, and reporting must be immediate so PEP can start within hours.
distractorExplanations.c: Every exposure is reported regardless of the source history, since infection status is often unknown or undisclosed.
distractorExplanations.d: HIV PEP should start within hours (ideally within 2, no later than 72); waiting up to a week is far too late.

prompt: Which is a work-practice control?

options.text: Recapping only with a one-handed scoop technique
Installing sharps containers at the point of use in each operatory
Using a safety syringe with a self-sheathing needle
Wearing puncture-resistant utility gloves during instrument cleanup

explanation: Work-practice controls change how tasks are performed to reduce exposure. Two-handed recapping is not acceptable; a safer mechanical method may also be used.

distractorExplanations.b: A sharps container is an engineering control that isolates the hazard, not a change in how the task is performed.
distractorExplanations.c: Safer sharps devices are engineering controls built into equipment; work-practice controls change worker behavior.
distractorExplanations.d: Utility gloves are personal protective equipment, a separate category from work-practice controls.

prompt: Eye wash stations should be

options.text: Available in the sterilization area, with squeeze bottles elsewhere instead
Available, accessible, and flushed/maintained per requirements
Located within a one-minute walk and flushed once each month
Installed at a sink and tested once a year during the OSHA review

explanation: Prompt irrigation capability is required for chemical exposures. This applies where corrosive chemicals are used.

distractorExplanations.a: Squeeze bottles are supplemental only and do not meet the required flushing flow or duration of a plumbed eyewash.
distractorExplanations.c: ANSI Z358.1 calls for reaching the station in about 10 seconds and activating plumbed units weekly.
distractorExplanations.d: Annual testing is far too infrequent; plumbed eyewashes are activated weekly to flush the line and verify flow.

prompt: Nitrous oxide occupational exposure is reduced by:

options.text: Turning off the scavenger during induction so the patient receives full flow
Checking equipment for leaks once a year, without a scavenging system
Scavenging systems, equipment checks, and appropriate ventilation/work practices
Room air purifiers with HEPA filters placed near the dental chair

explanation: Scavenging and maintenance protect staff from chronic N2O exposure.

distractorExplanations.a: Scavenging is needed throughout administration; switching it off releases exhaled nitrous into the operatory.
distractorExplanations.b: Leak checks are done regularly but do not replace scavenging, which captures exhaled gas at the source.
distractorExplanations.d: HEPA filters trap particles, not gases; they do not remove nitrous oxide from room air.

prompt: Which training topic is required under OSHA BBP for dental employees with exposure risk?

options.text: Hazard communication labeling, SDS use, and chemical spill cleanup
Fire extinguisher use, evacuation routes, and emergency action plans
Radiation safety, film handling, and dosimeter badge procedures
Modes of transmission, PPE use, and exposure response

explanation: BBP training covers exposure prevention and response; employers document training. Training also covers engineering and work-practice controls, and it must be documented.

Color-coded and filled to the very top before sealing to reduce waste-hauling costs
Lined with regular trash bags as long as the outer bin is labeled

prompt: Which statement about tuberculosis infection control in dentistry is correct?

options.text: Patients with latent TB infection should be treated in airborne isolation rooms
Patients with infectious TB should have elective care deferred
Patients with active TB can be treated routinely if staff wear surgical masks
Elective care can proceed once a patient with active TB has started medication

explanation: Airborne TB requires special handling beyond Standard Precautions alone. Urgent care uses airborne precautions or referral as appropriate.

distractorExplanations.a: Latent TB infection is not contagious; airborne precautions are for suspected or confirmed active TB disease.
distractorExplanations.c: Surgical masks do not filter TB droplet nuclei; active TB calls for deferral or treatment with N95 respirators and airborne precautions.
distractorExplanations.d: Starting treatment is not enough; elective care waits until a physician confirms the patient is no longer infectious.

options.text: Apply bleach to the wound, then report the incident after the shift ends

Letting the patient talk and mouth-breathe during nitrous sedation

Use vinyl gloves for patient care and latex utility gloves for instrument cleanup
